questions.q: What is the main limitation of metrics, even though they're cheap to store and great for dashboards?
options: Metrics cannot be collected in distributed systems at all
Metrics are aggregated summaries — they tell you that something is wrong, but not necessarily why
Metrics always require a distributed tracing system first
Metrics can only be collected once per day
questions.explain: Metrics summarize behavior over time (like error rate or latency), which is excellent for spotting trends and alerting, but doesn't by itself explain the root cause of a problem.

questions.q: Why does a distributed system specifically need distributed tracing, more so than a single-machine application?
options: Because a single request can touch many separate services running as separate processes, making it hard to see the full path without reconstructing it
Because distributed systems never produce any logs
Because tracing replaces the need for metrics entirely
Because single-machine applications cannot be debugged at all
questions.explain: In a distributed system, one user action can span many services across possibly many machines. Distributed tracing reconstructs that full journey, which is much harder to do by hand across scattered per-service logs.

questions.q: What is a correlation ID (trace ID) used for?
options: Encrypting sensitive log data
A unique identifier passed through every service a single request touches, used to reconstruct that request's complete path afterward
Limiting the rate of incoming requests
Electing a new leader node after a failure
questions.explain: A correlation ID is generated when a request enters the system and logged by every service it passes through, allowing all related log lines and trace spans to be reassembled into one coherent story.

questions.q: How does observability differ from monitoring?
options: They are identical concepts with different names
Monitoring watches predefined metrics against known thresholds; observability is the broader ability to investigate new, unanticipated questions using collected data
Observability only applies to single-machine systems
Monitoring requires distributed tracing, while observability does not use logs at all
questions.explain: Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask in advance (is a known metric over its threshold). Observability lets you explore questions you never anticipated, using the logs, metrics, and traces already being collected.

questions.q: Which combination correctly matches each observability pillar to its primary strength?
options: Logs = trends over time; Metrics = detailed individual events; Traces = aggregated dashboards
Logs = detailed individual events; Metrics = aggregated trends and alerting; Traces = a single request's path across services
Logs, metrics, and traces are all exactly the same type of data
Traces replace the need for both logs and metrics in every system
questions.explain: Logs capture detailed, discrete events; metrics aggregate numeric trends over time for dashboards and alerts; traces reconstruct the path and timing of one specific request across services.
